title: Strange History
blurb: True stories from the past that sound completely made up.

prompts.text: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great _____ of Giza.
Oxford University is older than the _____ Empire.
In 1518, a dancing plague saw hundreds of people dance for days on end in the city of _____.
Roman laundries, run by workers called fullers, cleaned togas by soaking them in stale _____.
The Hundred Years' War between England and France actually lasted _____ years.
The Eiffel Tower was only meant to stand for _____ years before being taken down.
In 1923, jockey Frank Hayes won a race in New York even though he was _____ when he crossed the line.
Abraham Lincoln has been honoured by America's national hall of fame for _____.
The horned helmets we picture on Vikings were popularised by costumes for 19th-century _____.
According to Herodotus, when a family's cat died, ancient Egyptians mourned by shaving off their _____.
Between 1912 and 1948, Olympic medals were also handed out for _____.
In 1919 a giant storage tank burst in Boston, flooding the streets with a wave of _____.
The 1859 standoff between the US and Britain over the San Juan Islands had only one casualty: a _____.
Russia's Peter the Great introduced a tax on _____.
The world's first webcam was set up at Cambridge University to keep an eye on a _____.
Woolly _____ were still alive on a remote Arctic island while the pyramids of Giza were being built.
In 1952, Albert Einstein was offered the job of president of _____.
Lord Byron was banned from keeping his dog at Cambridge, so he kept a pet _____ instead.
According to ancient writers, the Roman emperor Caligula planned to make his favourite _____ a consul.
Long before video games, Nintendo was founded in 1889 to make _____.
The Roman emperor Commodus loved to fight in the arena as a _____.
In medieval Europe, courts sometimes put _____ on trial for crimes.
Athletes at the ancient Greek Olympic Games competed _____.
In the 1904 Olympic marathon, the first man over the line was disqualified for riding part of the course in a _____.
The first person fined for speeding in Britain, in 1896, was doing about _____ miles per hour.
A brown oil paint popular with Victorian artists was made from ground-up Egyptian _____.
France carried out its last execution by guillotine in _____.
The Paris Catacombs hold the bones of roughly _____ million people.
The purple dye worn by Roman emperors was made from sea _____.
One of history's most powerful pirates, _____, commanded a huge fleet off the coast of China in the early 1800s.
Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 after leaving a dish of bacteria out while he went on _____.
Napoleon is remembered as tiny, but he was actually about _____ for a Frenchman of his time.
The Great Stink of 1858 finally forced _____ to fix the sewage-filled River Thames.
In 1859 a San Francisco businessman named Joshua Norton declared himself Emperor of the _____.
Operation Mincemeat in 1943 used a dead man carrying fake papers, given the false identity of Major William _____.
The airship Hindenburg burned in 1937 because it was filled with flammable _____ instead of helium.
According to a medieval Arab historian, Mali's Mansa Musa gave away so much gold on his 1324 pilgrimage that its value dropped in _____.
The Terracotta Army in China was found in 1974 by farmers who were digging a _____.
The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas split the newly explored world between Spain and _____.
The workers who built Egypt's pyramids were partly paid in daily rations of bread and _____.
George Washington's false teeth were never wooden; they were made from things like hippo ivory, gold and real _____.
In 897, Pope Stephen VI put the dug-up corpse of his predecessor, Pope _____, on trial.
France's King Charles VI spent years convinced that his body was made of _____.
The smaller bluestones of Stonehenge came from the Preseli Hills in _____.
